s: A few of the most popular tools in OpenFile use neural networks: the background remover, the image upscaler, the audio transcriber, the magic eraser and a couple more. People are often surprised that these run inside a browser tab with no server behind them. This post explains how that works, what happens the first time you use one, and why the experience is different on different devices.
A model is just a big file

A trained AI model is a file full of numbers, called weights, plus a description of the math that combines them. To run it you need two things: the file, and a runtime that can do that math quickly. On a server the runtime is usually PyTorch on a big GPU. In the browser, OpenFile uses ONNX Runtime Web, mostly through the Transformers.js library. It can run the same kind of model with WebAssembly on your CPU, or with WebGPU on your graphics card. So when you press a button in an AI tool, three things happen: the model file is fetched (once), the runtime loads it into memory, and your image or audio is pushed through it on your own hardware.

The panel below shows what this browser offers to AI tools: whether WebGPU is available, how many CPU cores the WebAssembly path can use, how much storage the site may use for models, and whether any OpenFile model files are already cached on this device.

Tool Model First download Background Remover ISNet through @imgly/background-removal, in a Best quality and a Faster version about 40 MB Image Upscaler Swin2SR, a 2x super-resolution transformer a few tens of MB Audio Transcriber Whisper by OpenAI, tiny or base about 40 MB or 80 MB Subtitle Translator NLLB-200 distilled, 200 languages about 900 MB Sizes are approximate and depend on the exact variant, but they give you a feel. A background remover costs about as much data as a short video clip. The translation model is a real download and worth doing on Wi-Fi.
Why the first run is slow and the second is fast

The first time, the tool shows a progress bar that says something like Downloading AI model (first run only). Once the file arrives, the OpenFile service worker stores it in a cache called openfile-models-v1. Every later run reads it from that cache instead of the network, so it starts in a second or two, and it works with no connection at all. Browsers can evict caches when a device runs very low on storage. If that ever happens, the next run simply downloads the model again. Nothing breaks.

Running a neural network is heavy. If it ran on the same thread that draws the page, the tab would freeze, buttons would stop responding, and the browser might offer to kill the page. So each AI tool runs its model in a Web Worker, a background thread with its own memory. The page only sends the input and receives progress messages and the result. The upscaler goes one step further and cuts big images into tiles. Each tile goes through the model on its own, with a little overlap so the seams do not show, and the progress bar counts tiles. This keeps memory use flat even for large photos and means you see real progress instead of a spinner that might be stuck.
WebGPU first, WebAssembly as the safety net

WebGPU lets a web page use the graphics card for general math, and neural networks are mostly the kind of math GPUs are built for. When it is available, the upscaler and the transcriber try it first, and the background remover can use it too. On a laptop with a decent GPU this is often several times faster than the CPU path. But WebGPU is new, and real devices are messy. Some browsers expose navigator.gpu but cannot give a working adapter. Some drivers fail halfway through a model. So OpenFile does not trust the flag alone: It asks for a real adapter before choosing the GPU path. If the GPU path fails during a run, the worker retries once on WebAssembly before giving up. If AI upscaling still fails, the upscaler falls back to a compatibility mode with careful multi-step resampling and sharpening, so you still get a usable bigger image instead of an error message. Good to know The tool always tells you which path it is on. The upscaler label reads Upscaling on GPU or Upscaling on CPU, so you know what speed to expect.

Background removal of a phone photo takes a few seconds. Transcribing a ten minute recording with Whisper tiny takes a minute or two on the CPU and less on a GPU. Upscaling a 1000 pixel image 2x takes seconds on a GPU and noticeably longer on CPU.

Phones work, but they have less memory and slow down when they get warm. Pick the Faster background model, keep images under about 2000 pixels on the long edge, and use Whisper tiny for transcripts. If a tool reports that it ran out of memory, a smaller input almost always fixes it. Keep the tab in the foreground while a long job runs. Browsers throttle background tabs, and on phones they may pause them entirely.
Why bother doing it this way

Cloud AI tools are fast because they run on expensive servers, and someone pays for those servers. Usually that someone is you, through a subscription, a watermark, or your data. Running the model locally costs a one-time download and some battery. In exchange your photos, voice memos and documents never leave your device, the tool keeps working offline, and it does not stop working when a company changes its pricing. If you want to try it, the Background Remover is the gentlest start: small model, quick result, and an easy way to see the first run and second run difference for yourself. The Magic Eraser and the Photo Enhancer use the same approach.

Every bank lets you download your transactions, but the download menu often reads like alphabet soup: OFX, QFX, QIF, CSV, CAMT.053, MT940. Pick the wrong one and your money app refuses it, or your spreadsheet shows dates as random numbers. I went through all of these while building the Money and Finance tools in OpenFile, so here is what each format is, which one to choose, and how to convert between them without sending your statement to a website you do not know.

A bank statement is a list of rows: a date, an amount, some text about who you paid, and sometimes a reference and a running balance. That sounds simple, yet each format stores it differently. Some put the sign on the amount, some use a separate debit and credit column, some use letters like D and C. Dates come as 20261003, 03/10/2026 or 10/03/2026, and the last two mean different days depending on the country. A good converter has to guess these things correctly, and let you fix them when it guesses wrong.

Format Where it comes from Good for OFX / QFX Most US, UK and Indian banks, card issuers Importing into money apps, keeps IDs so imports do not double QIF Older Quicken exports, many apps still read it Simple imports, easy to read by eye CSV Every bank, every country Spreadsheets, but each bank uses its own columns CAMT.053 European banks (ISO 20022 XML) Detailed SEPA data: names, IBANs, remittance text MT940 SWIFT format, business and older EU banking Accounting software, very compact

OFX stands for Open Financial Exchange. Version 1 looks like HTML with tags that are never closed, version 2 is proper XML. QFX is the same thing with a few extra fields for one money app, and QBO is another variant for accounting software. Each transaction sits in a block called STMTTRN with a date, an amount, a name, an optional memo, and a FITID, which is a unique id. That id is the clever part: when you import the same file twice, the app sees the same ids and skips the copies.

QIF is a plain text format from the early days of personal finance software. Each line starts with one letter: D for date, T for amount, P for payee, M for memo, and a caret on its own line ends the record. It has no unique ids and the dates are usually month first, which is why QIF imports sometimes land in the wrong month for people outside the US.

CSV is the format everyone has and nobody agrees on. One bank calls the column Narration, another Details, another Description. Some have a single Amount column, others split it into Withdrawal and Deposit. Many put a few title lines above the real header. When you open a CSV in Bank Statement Converter, it looks for the header row, matches columns by their names, and checks the dates to decide if they are day first or month first. You can change any of those choices in the side panel and the table updates at once.

If you bank in Europe, you may see CAMT.053, which is part of the ISO 20022 standard. It is XML with a lot of detail: who paid, their IBAN, the remittance text, booking and value dates. MT940 is the older SWIFT message with lines that start with codes like:61: for a transaction and:86: for its description. Both are great for accounting, and both are hard to read in a spreadsheet without converting first.
Try it: paste a bank file
The box below runs the same parser the tools use. Pick a sample, then edit the text and watch the table change. Change a minus sign, break a date, or delete a closing tag.

For a money or budgeting app: OFX if your bank offers it. The ids prevent duplicates. QIF is the fallback. For a spreadsheet: CSV, or any format converted to Excel with the converter. Excel output keeps amounts as real numbers, so sums work straight away. For your accountant: ask them. Many prefer CAMT.053 or MT940 in Europe, and OFX or CSV elsewhere. Only a PDF available: use PDF Statement to CSV. It rebuilds lines from the positions of the text on each page, keeps the lines that start with a date and hold an amount, and works out money in or out from the running balance. If your app only accepts OFX but your bank only gives CSV, CSV to OFX writes a proper OFX 2.2 file. Each row gets a stable id made from its date, amount and text, so re-importing the same month does not double anything.
What to do once it is converted

Converting is usually the first step, not the goal. Two tools help with the next one. Statement Analyzer shows money in and out by month, your top payees, and a list of payments that repeat at the same amount, which is a quick way to find a forgotten subscription. AI Transaction Categorizer labels each row as groceries, transport, bills and so on. It tries simple keyword rules first, and for names it has never seen it can run a small sentence model (MiniLM, about 25 MB) in a background worker. On a laptop without a GPU it starts in rules only mode, so nothing heavy loads unless you ask for it. Check the totals Whatever tool you use, compare the total in and total out against the statement itself before you file anything. A wrong date order or a flipped sign is easy to miss in a long list.
Why I keep this on my own device

A statement shows where you live, where you shop, what you earn and who you send money to. Many online converters ask you to upload exactly that. Every finance tool in OpenFile reads the file inside your browser tab. You can open the page, switch off Wi-Fi, and convert a year of statements. Nothing is stored after you close the tab. Limits Bank exports are not always standard. If a file does not open, the CSV route almost always works, because you can point the tool at the right columns yourself. Encrypted PDF statements need their password first, which you can remove with Unlock PDF.

Last month a friend who runs a small online store sent me 200 product photos. Each one needed the same treatment: resize, add a small watermark, remove location data, convert to WebP, and bundle them up. Doing that one by one would take an afternoon. With the Workspace it took a couple of minutes.

I start by writing the steps down in order. Order matters. Resizing first makes every later step faster because there are fewer pixels to work on. Resize so the long edge is 1600 pixels. Add a small text watermark in the corner. Strip EXIF data, which can include GPS location. Convert to WebP at quality 80. Download everything as one ZIP.
Toggle steps on and off, then run it. This is a simulation, but the real Workspace looks and behaves the same way.

Open the Workspace, drop the folder of photos, and add the steps from the list on the left. Each step has its own options. I run it on two or three test photos first, check the results, and only then run the whole batch.

Once it looks right, save the pipeline as a recipe. Next month, when the next batch arrives, load the recipe, drop the files, press run. Recipes are stored in your browser and are included when you export your settings. Name recipes after the job, not the steps. "Store photos" is easier to find later than "resize watermark webp".

There is no upload. 200 photos at 5 MB each is a gigabyte, which would take a long time to send to a server. Here the bytes never leave the machine, so the only limit is how fast your CPU can encode images.

A lot of my week is moving data between shapes. An API returns JSON and a colleague wants it in Excel. A data export comes as Parquet and I just want to look at it. A spreadsheet needs to become a JSON config. Each of these formats makes different promises, and most conversion bugs come from forgetting what a format cannot hold. This post is a field guide to CSV, JSON, Excel and Parquet, and how to convert between them without losing anything important.

Format Shape Types Best at CSV one flat table none, everything is text exchange between any two programs JSON nested objects and lists string, number, true or false, null APIs, configs, anything nested Excel (XLSX) several sheets of cells numbers, dates, text, formulas, formatting people who want to look and edit Parquet one table, stored by column rich: integers, decimals, timestamps, nested large datasets and analytics

Comma separated values is the oldest and simplest: one line per row, commas between cells. It has no official types. The text 007 and the number 7 look the same to a program reading it unless it guesses. A cell containing a comma or a line break must be wrapped in double quotes, and a quote inside a quoted cell is written twice. Most broken CSV files I see break one of those two rules.

JSON can nest: an order can contain a customer, which contains an address, which contains a list of phone numbers. It has real types for numbers, true and false, and null. It has no date type, so dates travel as strings, and no comments.

An XLSX file is actually a ZIP of XML files. It holds multiple sheets, formulas, formatting and real dates. A sheet can hold at most 1,048,576 rows, which sounds like a lot until you open a log export.

Parquet stores data by column instead of by row. All the values of one column sit together, which compresses very well (a column of country codes is mostly repeats) and lets analytics tools read only the columns they need. It carries a proper schema with types. It is binary, so you cannot open it in a text editor.

Edit the CSV on the left. Notice that the quoted cell with a comma stays in one column, numbers and true or false become real JSON values, and a dotted header like address.zip can become a nested object.

Nested data into a flat table

JSON to CSV only works cleanly when every record has the same shape. Nested objects can be flattened into columns like address.city. Lists are harder: a customer with three phone numbers either becomes three columns, one cell with the numbers joined, or three rows. None is wrong, but pick one on purpose.

Going from CSV to anything typed means guessing. Postal codes and phone numbers with leading zeros become numbers and lose the zero. Long ID numbers turn into scientific notation in Excel. Strings like 1-2 or MARCH1 become dates. When I care, I keep those columns as text, or convert through JSON where strings stay strings. The Excel date trap Opening a CSV by double-clicking it in Excel lets Excel guess types for every column, and it may silently change gene names, product codes and IDs into dates. Import through the data tab with column types set, or edit the file in the CSV editor first.

If accented letters or non-Latin scripts turn into garbage, the file and the program disagree about the encoding. UTF-8 is the right choice almost everywhere. Older versions of Excel only recognise UTF-8 in a CSV when the file starts with a byte order mark. If a file looks wrong, Text Encoding Detector and Converter can tell you what it really is.

A 2 GB CSV is not a spreadsheet anymore. Converting it to Parquet usually makes it several times smaller and much faster to query. Going the other way, filter the Parquet file in the viewer first and export only the rows you need. When I get JSON from an API and only need a few fields, I trim it first with JSONPath and JSONata Tester, then convert. Smaller input, cleaner table. Private by default Exports from work systems are full of customer names, emails and order histories. All of these tools parse files in your browser with open source libraries such as Papa Parse, SheetJS, hyparquet and sql.js, and nothing is uploaded. That is the main reason I stopped using random online converters for this.

I read a lot on a phone and an old e-reader, and the files come from everywhere: EPUBs from publishers that sell DRM-free books, MOBI files from an old Kindle library, PDFs of papers, and comic archives from friends. Each format behaves differently on a small screen. This post explains the main ebook formats, the one idea that matters most, and how to convert between them without uploading your library anywhere.
The one idea: reflowable or fixed

Every ebook format falls into one of two families. Reflowable books store text and its structure (chapters, headings, paragraphs) but not where each line falls on a page. The reader app lays out the text for your screen and your font size. EPUB, MOBI, AZW3 and FB2 work this way. Fixed layout files store exact pages. A PDF page looks the same on a 27 inch monitor and on a phone, which means on the phone you zoom and scroll sideways. PDF and comic archives work this way. Drag the width slider below down to phone size and you will see the difference in a second. For novels and most non-fiction, reflowable wins. For anything where layout matters, such as comics, cookbooks with photos next to steps, or academic papers with equations and figures, fixed layout is usually the better choice.

Format What it is Where it shows up EPUB an open standard: a ZIP of HTML chapters, CSS, images and a contents file Kobo, Apple Books, Google Play Books, most reader apps, and Kindle through Send to Kindle MOBI, AZW, AZW3 Amazon's older formats, AZW3 also called KF8 older Kindle libraries and downloads FB2 FictionBook, a single XML file popular in Eastern Europe and Russia CBZ, CBR, CB7 a ZIP, RAR or 7z archive of page images comics and manga PDF fixed pages papers, manuals, textbooks
Why EPUB is the safe choice

EPUB is an open format maintained as a web standard, and under the hood it is just a website in a ZIP file. That makes it easy to repair, easy to edit and likely to stay readable for decades. Amazon also moved towards it: Send to Kindle accepts EPUB and converts it for the device, and Amazon has phased out MOBI uploads there. So when someone asks me which format to convert a book into, the answer is nearly always EPUB.

It reads Kindle and EPUB files with foliate-js, the engine behind the Foliate reader, collects chapters, images and metadata into one book model on your device, and writes a fresh EPUB 3 or whichever output you picked. Some conversions I do regularly: Old MOBI or AZW3 to EPUB before moving a library to a Kobo or to Apple Books. EPUB to PDF when I want to print a chapter or annotate it with a stylus. EPUB to PDF does just that. EPUB to Markdown or plain text to quote passages in notes, or to run a long text through other tools. Word to EPUB for friends who write and want to read their own draft on an e-reader. DRM Books bought from most big stores are protected with DRM, which locks them to an account. OpenFile does not remove DRM and cannot open protected files. Everything here is for DRM-free books, which many publishers, bundles and public domain libraries offer.

This is the hard direction, and it is worth understanding why. A PDF does not know what a paragraph is. It knows that a word sits at a certain position on a page. To make a reflowable book, PDF to EPUB has to rebuild the structure: it groups text into headings, paragraphs, lists and tables, splits chapters at headings (or every few pages if there are none), and packs the result as an EPUB 3 with a contents list and a cover. On a clean, text-based PDF such as a report or a novel exported from a word processor, the result reads well. On a two column scientific paper or a magazine layout, expect some oddities. Footnotes, page headers and figures placed in the margin are the usual troublemakers. In those cases I just keep the PDF. If the PDF is a scan, there is no text to rebuild. Run OCR PDF first, then convert.
Fixing a book without converting it

Sometimes the file is fine but the details are wrong: a missing cover, the author's name in the title field, a series number nobody filled in. EPUB Editor changes the cover, title, author, series and tags. It edits the EPUB package in place, so chapters, fonts and styles are left untouched. It can also shrink oversized images, which helps old e-readers that struggle with 5 MB cover pictures, and it can merge several books into one with a combined table of contents. I use that for short story collections that were sold as separate files.

Comic archives are just folders of images in a ZIP (CBZ), RAR (CBR) or 7z (CB7). Comic Converter sorts pages in natural order, so page 10 comes after page 9 and not after page 1, and turns them into a PDF or a CBZ. It can also resize and recompress pages, which can take a 300 MB scan down to something a tablet opens without stuttering.

You do not have to convert at all if you only want to read. E-book Reader opens EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, FB2 and CBZ in the browser, with themes, search and a table of contents. Your reading position is saved on this device only. On a laptop it is a pleasant way to read a long document without installing anything, and installed as an app it works offline on a flight.

File formats can feel like alphabet soup. PDF, DOCX, WebP, HEIC, MKV. Each one exists for a reason, and picking the right one saves space, time and headaches. This guide covers the formats I see most often, with an explorer you can click through.

For video and audio it helps to know two words. A container is the box: MP4, MKV, WebM, MOV. A codec is how the picture or sound inside is compressed: H.264, VP9, AV1, AAC, Opus. Two MP4 files can contain very different codecs, which is why one plays and the other does not.
Sending something that must look the same everywhere: PDF. Something people will edit: DOCX, or Markdown for technical docs. Tables of data: CSV for exchange, XLSX when you need formulas.
Photos: WebP or JPG. Screenshots and logos: PNG or SVG. iPhone photos to share with Windows users: convert HEIC to JPG with HEIC Converter.
Sharing video: MP4 with H.264. It plays nearly everywhere. Web video with small files: WebM. Music to keep: FLAC. Music to share: AAC or MP3.

Convert at the end of your work, not in the middle. Every lossy conversion throws away a bit of quality, so going JPG to WebP to JPG makes things worse each time. Keep an original in a lossless format if you plan to edit it later.

Four photo formats come up again and again in messages I get: HEIC, because iPhones save it and Windows does not always open it; JPG, because it opens everywhere; AVIF, because web developers keep recommending it; and JPEG XL, because people read that it is the best of all and then cannot open the file. Here is how they compare, and which one I actually use for what.

Sending a photo to someone: JPG. It is not the smallest, but it opens on every device made in the last thirty years. Photos on a website: AVIF with a JPG or WebP fallback, or just WebP if you want one file. Your own archive: keep whatever your camera or phone made. Converting an original to another lossy format only loses detail. Looking ahead: JPEG XL is technically excellent, but support is still patchy, so do not make it the only copy you share.

JPEG dates from 1992. It splits the picture into 8 by 8 pixel blocks and stores each block as a mix of wave patterns, throwing away the fine detail your eyes are least likely to miss. It has no transparency, no animation and only 8 bits per channel. Its superpower is that everything opens it.

HEIC is a HEIF container holding images compressed with HEVC, the same codec used for a lot of 4K video. Apple made it the default camera format on iPhone in 2017. At the same visual quality, a HEIC is often around half the size of a JPG, and it can hold extras such as depth maps, bursts and the still part of a Live Photo. The problem is support. HEVC is covered by patents with licensing fees, so most browsers and many apps never added it. Safari opens HEIC. Chrome and Firefox do not, and on Windows you may need an extra codec from the Store. That is why HEIC is the format people most often need to convert.

AVIF is the same idea as HEIC, but built on AV1, a royalty-free video codec from the Alliance for Open Media. It compresses about as well as HEIC or better, supports transparency, HDR and animation, and every major browser decodes it today. The cost is encoding speed: AVIF takes noticeably longer to create than JPG or WebP, and very large AVIFs can be slow to encode on a phone.

JPEG XL (file extension.jxl) is the newest of the four and was designed as a true successor to JPG. It compresses well across the whole quality range, supports lossless, transparency, HDR and very large images, and decodes progressively, so a blurry preview appears first and sharpens as the file loads. It also has a unique trick: it can repack an existing JPG losslessly, about 20 percent smaller, and give back the original JPG bit for bit. Support is the open question. Safari added JPEG XL in version 17. Chrome removed its experimental support in 2023, and the Chromium project has since said it would take it back with a new decoder, but at the time of writing you cannot count on a random visitor's browser opening a.jxl file. Use the check below to see where your browser stands.

JPG HEIC AVIF JPEG XL Typical size at similar quality largest about half of JPG about half of JPG or less about half of JPG or less Transparency no yes yes yes Animation no image sequences yes yes HDR and more than 8 bits no yes yes yes Lossless mode no rarely used yes yes, and lossless JPG repacking Opens in browsers all Safari only all major ones Safari, others vary Royalty free yes no yes yes The size column is a rough guide. Real savings depend on the photo, the encoder and the quality setting, and they shrink at very high quality.

That means it works even in a browser that cannot save those formats on its own. That gives excellent results, but it is not the bit-exact JPG repacking described above, which needs the reference command line tool. If you want zero additional loss from a JPG, use lossless mode, and expect a bigger file than the lossy one.

Converting back and forth. HEIC to JPG to AVIF to JPG loses a little detail at every lossy step. Convert once, from the original. Judging by the extension. Some apps save a JPG with a.heic name or the other way round. If a file will not open, check what it really is with File Type Identifier. Forgetting metadata. All four formats can carry EXIF data, including GPS location. Conversion in OpenFile does not add anything, but if you share photos publicly, strip location with EXIF Viewer and Remover. On an iPhone you can switch the camera to Most Compatible in Settings, Camera, Formats, and it will shoot JPG instead of HEIC. I leave it on HEIC to save space and convert only the photos I share.

People ask me one question more than any other: "Where do my files go?" The honest answer is that they stay in the browser tab you have open. This post explains what that means, how it works, and how you can check it yourself without trusting me.

When you drop a file into an OpenFile tool, the browser reads it into memory in that tab. The tool does its work with JavaScript, WebAssembly and the Canvas API on your own CPU or GPU. The result is turned into a download link that points at memory in the same tab. At no point is the file sent to a server. There is no account, no upload queue and no "processing on our side". There is not even a backend that could receive your files. The site is a set of static files on a CDN.
What actually happens to a file

Reading. The browser gives the page a File object. Reading it with arrayBuffer() copies the bytes into the tab's memory. Processing. A library does the work locally. For PDFs that is pdf-lib and PDF.js. For video it is ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. For background removal it is a small neural network running with WebAssembly or WebGPU. Output. The result becomes a Blob. The page creates an object URL for it and your browser saves it like any other download. Cleanup. Close the tab and the memory is gone. Nothing is written to a server, and the only things kept on your device are your settings, favorites and history, which you can clear in Settings.
The demo below reads a file and computes its SHA-256 fingerprint. It also counts how many network requests the page made while it worked. Pick something large to make the point.

Some tools need a heavy engine the first time you use them. Video tools download ffmpeg (about 30 MB). OCR downloads Tesseract and a language file. AI tools download a model. These are downloads to your device, not uploads from it, and the service worker caches them so later runs work offline. Good to know If you want to be sure, load a tool once, switch on airplane mode, and use it. Most tools keep working with no connection at all.
The few things that are not local

I want to be precise here. The fonts on the site come from a font CDN. The Status page calls a tiny health check endpoint. Neither of these ever sees your files. If you self host OpenFile you can remove both.
Why I built it this way

Most free file tools on the web upload your document to a server, process it there, and ask you to trust that it gets deleted. For a payslip, a contract or a passport scan, that trust is a lot to ask. Browsers today are fast enough that the upload step is simply not needed for most jobs, so I removed it. The code is open source under the MIT license. If you want to read exactly what a tool does, every tool lives in its own file in the repository.

Image compression sounds technical, but the idea is simple: store a picture using fewer bytes. The trick is deciding what to throw away. This post explains the main ideas in plain words, and there is a slider you can drag to see the result for yourself.

Lossless compression keeps every pixel exactly. PNG works this way. It is like zipping a file: smaller, but you get back exactly what you put in. Lossy compression throws away detail your eyes are unlikely to notice. JPG, WebP and AVIF can all work this way. The quality setting decides how much gets thrown away.

The image below is drawn in your browser and encoded with your browser's own JPG and WebP encoders. Lower the quality and watch the fine lines and the small text first. Then try one of your own photos.

Color detail. Eyes are more sensitive to brightness than to color, so encoders store color at lower resolution. Fine texture. The image is split into small blocks and each block is described with a few wave patterns. High quality keeps more of them. Sharp edges. Text and thin lines get soft halos at low quality. That is why screenshots look bad as JPG.

Photos for the web: WebP at quality 75 to 82. AVIF if you want the smallest files and can wait for slower encoding. Screenshots, logos, text: PNG, or lossless WebP. Maximum compatibility: JPG at quality 80 to 85.

The biggest saving is often not the quality setting at all. A 4000 pixel photo shown at 1200 pixels wastes most of its bytes. Run Image Resizer first, then Image Compressor. Set a default image quality in Settings. Every tool that does not choose its own quality will use it.

GIF is a format from 1987 that refuses to go away. It has no sound, a limit of 256 colours per frame and compression that was clever for dial-up modems. Yet it still plays inline almost everywhere: chat apps, issue trackers, READMEs, email newsletters. So when I need a short loop of a screen recording or a funny moment from a video, I still make a GIF. Here is how to make a good one that is not 40 MB.

A video codec like H.264 stores one full picture now and then and, between them, only the changes, using motion prediction. GIF stores frames much more simply. Each frame is compressed on its own with LZW, the same family of compression as a ZIP file. Areas that do not change between frames can be skipped, but anything that moves is stored again in full. So the size of a GIF depends on four things, and you control all of them: the width, the frame rate, the length, and the number of colours. Play with the planner below to get a feel for it.

Every second you remove is a second you do not have to encode, so cut before you convert. I open the video in Video Trimmer, find the exact moment, and keep only that. Two to six seconds is the sweet spot for a reaction GIF. For a product demo or a bug report, up to fifteen seconds is fine if the frame is small. If your clip is long, you can also set start and end times directly in Video to GIF. Trimming first is still faster, because the GIF tool then only has to decode the part you want.

This matters most because pixels grow with the square of the width. A 960 pixel GIF has four times the pixels of a 480 pixel one. Video to GIF offers 320, 480, 640 and 800 pixels or the original size. For chat I use 480. For documentation, where text on screen must be readable, 640 or 800.

Video is usually 24 to 60 frames per second. A GIF rarely needs more than 10 to 15. At 12 frames per second motion still looks smooth, and you store a fifth of the frames a 60 fps screen recording has. GIF timing is stored in hundredths of a second, so rates that divide 100 neatly, such as 10, 20 and 25, play the most evenly. Most browsers also slow down frames shorter than 0.02 seconds, so very high rates are wasted anyway.

Each GIF frame can have at most 256 colours. A good converter does not use a fixed palette: it looks at the whole clip and builds the 256 colours that represent it best. OpenFile does this with ffmpeg's palettegen and paletteuse filters, which is why you see Building palette and encoding GIF while it works. Dithering decides how to fake colours that are not in the palette. None gives flat bands, which looks great on screen recordings with solid backgrounds and keeps files small. Pattern gives an ordered, slightly retro texture. Smooth spreads the error around and looks best on real footage like skin and sky, but it adds noise that makes the file bigger.
Forever is what people expect. Play once or 3 times is good for a GIF in a presentation, where an endless loop can be distracting.
Step 3: make it smaller after the fact

If the result is still too large for where it is going (Discord, GitHub and many forums have upload limits), run it through GIF Compressor. It stores only the part of each frame that changed, merges identical frames, can drop every other frame, reduce colours, and has a target size mode that keeps trying settings until the file fits.
When a GIF is the wrong choice

If the place you are posting accepts video, a short MP4 is usually a tenth of the size of the same GIF, with full colour and smooth motion. Most social apps actually convert uploaded GIFs into videos behind the scenes for exactly this reason. For a website you control, an animated WebP or AVIF gives full colour at a fraction of the size. Animated WebP Maker and Animated Image Converter make both from the same clip. For a lossless loop with true transparency, APNG is the better format. It works in every modern browser. For anything with sound, use video. GIF has no audio at all. Captions and stickers Want a caption on the loop, like a classic reaction GIF? Make the GIF first, then add text with Add Text and Images to GIF. Text added after the palette is built stays sharp instead of getting dithered.
My recipe for a bug report GIF

Record the screen with the Screen Recorder, only the window that matters. Trim to the few seconds that show the bug. Video to GIF at 640 pixels, 10 fps, 256 colours, no dithering. If it is over 10 MB, GIF Compressor with target size. It usually lands between 1 and 4 MB, the text stays readable, and it plays right inside the issue. Everything happens in the browser with ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly, so the recording never leaves your machine, which matters when the screen shows a client's dashboard.

MIDI files confuse people because they are music files that contain no sound. A three minute song in MIDI can be 20 KB, smaller than a single photo, and it sounds completely different depending on what plays it. Once you see what is inside, that makes perfect sense. This post explains MIDI in plain words, with a small piano roll you can play, and shows how to turn a MIDI file into a normal audio file.

MIDI, the Musical Instrument Digital Interface, was agreed by instrument makers in 1983 so that keyboards, drum machines and computers from different brands could talk to each other. It does not carry audio. It carries instructions: start playing this note now, this hard; stop playing it now; switch to a different instrument; move this knob. A.mid file, a Standard MIDI File, is a recording of those instructions with timing attached. Think of it as sheet music that a computer can read exactly. Whatever reads it, a synthesizer, a phone, a browser, decides what each note actually sounds like.

Here is the opening of a well known melody stored the MIDI way: a list of note numbers, start times and lengths. Press Play, then change the tempo, transpose it, or switch the sound. Notice that none of those changes touch the notes themselves, only how they are performed.

Every key gets a number from 0 to 127. Middle C is 60. Each step up is one semitone, so 72 is the C one octave higher. The A above middle C, the note orchestras tune to at 440 Hz, is 69. Transposing a song is literally adding the same number to every note, which is what the slider in the demo does.
Each note also has a velocity from 1 to 127, how hard the key was hit. A good synthesizer plays a soft note quieter and often with a different tone.

Times are stored in ticks, and the file says how many ticks make one beat. A separate tempo setting says how long a beat lasts. Because of this split, changing the tempo of a MIDI file is clean and instant, no time stretching artifacts, unlike speeding up an MP3.

A file can contain several tracks, usually one per instrument. Each note travels on one of 16 channels, and a program change message picks an instrument for that channel. The General MIDI standard fixes a list of 128 instruments, so program 1 is always an acoustic grand piano and 41 is always a violin, and it reserves channel 10 for drums, where each note number is a different drum rather than a pitch.
Why the same file sounds different everywhere

Since the file only says play a violin, the quality depends on the violin sound available. A professional sample library makes it sound like a real orchestra. A basic phone synth makes it sound like a 1990s video game. Neither is wrong. They are reading the same sheet music.

MIDI Player and Converter opens.mid,.midi and.kar karaoke files. It reads them with the open source @tonejs/midi library and plays them through a small built-in synthesizer on the Web Audio API. The piano roll shows every note as a bar, with a playhead that follows the music. The track list shows each instrument and its note count. Mute tracks to hear one part on its own, which is great for learning the bass line or a piano part. Speed and volume controls apply as you listen. Render to WAV, MP3 or OGG to get a normal audio file you can send to anyone. Rendering uses an offline audio context: the browser computes the audio as fast as it can instead of in real time, so a four minute song usually exports in a few seconds. Honest about the sound The built-in synthesizer is small on purpose. It shapes simple waveforms per instrument family (piano, strings, brass and so on) and has its own drum sounds, so the whole thing loads instantly and works offline. It sounds clear and musical, but it is not a sampled concert grand. If you need realistic instruments, open the MIDI file in a music program with a good sound library.
Things people do with MIDI files

Practise. Mute the part you play and play along with the rest at a slower speed. Make a backing track. Render to MP3, then cut it to length in Audio Editor and Trimmer. Make a video. Render to audio, then use Audio to Video Visualizer to add a cover and an animated waveform for a social post. Change format for a device. Some older phones and car stereos want a specific format. Render to WAV, then convert with Audio Converter. Old game soundtracks, ringtones and karaoke libraries are full of MIDI files. If a.kar file has lyrics embedded, they are stored as timed text events in the same file, right next to the notes.

People sometimes ask for MP3 to MIDI. That direction is much harder, because the tool has to listen to mixed audio and guess every note, a problem called transcription. It works reasonably for a single clean instrument and poorly for a full band. OpenFile does not do it today, and I would rather say so than ship something that gives disappointing results.

A friend who is an architect once sent me a floor plan as a DXF file and asked me to check one measurement. I did not have AutoCAD, and the free viewers I found either wanted an account or an upload. That annoyance turned into two OpenFile tools: a DXF viewer and a CAD converter. This post explains what DXF actually is, how the tools read it, and the jobs they are good for.

AutoCAD has two file formats. DWG is its native format: compact, binary and closed. Other programs read it by reverse engineering, and its details change between AutoCAD versions. DXF, the Drawing Exchange Format, was introduced by Autodesk in the early 1980s precisely so other programs could exchange drawings with AutoCAD. Its specification is published, and nearly every CAD, laser cutting, CNC and GIS program can import and export it. So the practical advice is simple: if someone sends you a DWG, ask for a DXF, or save one yourself from AutoCAD, LibreCAD, FreeCAD, QCAD or any other CAD program. Save As, then pick DXF.
A DXF file is just text

The most common form of DXF is plain text made of pairs of lines. The first line of each pair is a group code, a number that says what the next line means. The second is the value. A few codes you will see everywhere: 0 starts a new entity and names its type, such as LINE, CIRCLE, ARC, LWPOLYLINE or TEXT. 8 is the layer name. 10 and 20 are the X and Y of the first point, 11 and 21 the second point of a line. 40 is a radius for circles and arcs, or the height for text. Below is a tiny but real DXF entities section: a rectangle on a WALLS layer, a circle on FIXTURES and a dimension line. Change a number on the left and the drawing updates. Click a layer name to hide it. A real drawing has thousands of entities plus a header with units and settings, a tables section that defines layers, line types and text styles, and blocks, which are reusable groups of entities such as a door or a chair placed many times. But the principle is exactly what you see above.

DXF Viewer parses the file with the open source dxf library, which expands blocks, arcs, splines and polylines into plain line work. Then it draws everything with Canvas 2D, grouped by layer. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, and press 0 to fit the whole drawing on screen. Toggle layers in the side panel. Floor plans often have separate layers for walls, furniture, electrical and dimensions, and hiding the clutter makes them far easier to read. Use the ruler to measure the distance between two points in the drawing's own units. Save the visible layers as SVG, which you can drop into a document or a web page.

A DXF stores coordinates as plain numbers. Whether 1 means a millimetre, an inch or a metre is a drawing setting, and older files sometimes do not say. If a measurement looks a thousand times too big or too small, the drawing is probably in millimetres and you were expecting metres. Check what the sender intended before you order materials based on it.

Most people who receive a drawing just want to look at it or print it. CAD to PDF, SVG and PNG handles that: PDF output is real vector paths, built with jsPDF and svg2pdf, so lines stay sharp at any zoom and print cleanly. You pick the page size. SVG is grouped by layer, which is handy if you want to restyle it later. PNG and JPG are rendered at the width you choose, good for chat or email. Two options I use a lot: hiding layers before export, so a client gets the plan without the construction notes, and print-friendly black lines. CAD drawings often use light colours meant for a dark screen, and yellow lines on white paper are nearly invisible. The black lines option turns everything dark for printing. For a laser cutter or a vinyl cutter, export SVG with only the cut layer visible. Most cutter software imports SVG directly, and you avoid cutting your own dimension lines.

It does not open DWG. That would mean shipping a large reverse engineered library, and DXF covers the need. It is a viewer and converter, not an editor. You can hide, measure and export, but not move walls. 3D solids inside a DXF are shown as their edges. For real 3D models, use 3D Model Viewer, which opens STL, OBJ, GLB, 3MF, FBX and many more. Why local matters here Drawings are often confidential: unreleased buildings, product designs, the layout of someone's home. With these tools the file is parsed in your browser tab and never uploaded, so you can open a client drawing on a laptop at a site visit without wondering where a copy ended up.

I handle a lot of PDFs: forms, invoices, scanned notes, slides people export without thinking about size. Over time I picked up a few habits that make this work quick. Here are the ten I use the most.
Almost every PDF tool in OpenFile accepts ranges like 1-3, 7, 10-. A dash with no end means "to the last page". Once this is in your fingers, splitting and extracting takes seconds.
Merging and then fixing the order is slower than getting each file right first. Open Organize PDF, drag pages into place, delete the blank ones, then merge.
Compression works best on the final document. If you compress, then add pages, then compress again, you lose quality twice. Make Compress PDF your final step.
4. Scans are images, treat them that way
A scanned PDF is mostly pictures of pages. That is why scans are big and why compression helps them the most. Lowering image resolution to 150 DPI is usually invisible on screen.
5. Run OCR to make scans searchable
OCR PDF adds an invisible text layer on top of each scanned page. The page looks the same, but now you can search it, select text and copy it.
Sign PDF lets you draw, type or upload a signature and place it on any page. Nothing is uploaded, which matters a lot for contracts.
Drawing a black box over text in most viewers does not remove the text underneath. The redaction tool rasterizes the area so the original text is really gone.
8. Split big files by size for email
Many mail servers reject attachments over 20 or 25 MB. Splitting into chunks by page count is usually the fastest way under the limit.
Every tool gives you a new file and never changes the one you dropped in. I still keep a copy of the original in a folder called "source" before I start.
If you do the same steps every week, the Workspace can run them as one recipe on a whole batch. Press Ctrl K (or Cmd K) anywhere on the site to jump straight to a tool by name.

Text to speech is useful for proofreading, for accessibility, and for turning notes into something you can listen to on a walk. Most online options send your text to a cloud service. OpenFile does it on your device.

Every major browser has a Speech Synthesis API that uses the voices installed on your operating system. On Windows, macOS, Android and iOS these voices are often very good, and they cost nothing to load.

Some setups have no voices at all. Many Linux desktops and some privacy focused browsers report zero. Before, the tool simply showed "Voice 0 of 0", which was not helpful. Now, when no system voice is available, Text to Speech switches to a neural voice engine that runs in the tab. It is based on the open Kokoro model and runs with WebAssembly, or WebGPU when your browser has it. The model downloads once (around 90 MB), shows its progress, and is cached for next time.

You can also choose the engine yourself. System voices start instantly. The neural engine sounds more natural with some voices and lets you download the result as a WAV file, which the system engine cannot do because browsers do not expose its audio.
If you need speech turned into text, Audio Transcriber runs the Whisper model locally. Same idea: the audio never leaves your device.

Receipts pile up in wallets, drawers and photo galleries. For expense claims, taxes or just a monthly budget, I want them as rows in a spreadsheet: the shop, the date, the tax and the total. Receipt apps do this well, but most of them upload your photos to a server and some keep them. So I built AI Receipt Scanner to do the whole job on the device. Here is how it works, what it gets right, and where you still need to check its work.

Text recognition works best on dark text on a light background with good contrast. Phone photos of thermal paper are often the opposite: grey, curled and lit from one side. Before reading, the tool shrinks the photo so the longest side is 1600 pixels (2400 in Best mode), turns it grey, and stretches the contrast so the darkest pixel becomes black and the lightest becomes white. That simple step makes a big difference on faded receipts, and the smaller size makes reading faster.
Step 2: read the text with OCR

The reading is done by Tesseract, an open source OCR engine that uses a small LSTM neural network trained to recognise lines of text. In the browser it runs as WebAssembly inside a Web Worker, which is a background thread. That has two good effects: The page stays responsive while it reads, and the Cancel button stops it straight away. It needs no graphics card. It runs on the CPU of any laptop or phone. The language model downloads the first time, about 4 to 15 MB per language, and the browser keeps it for next time. You can pick English, English with Hindi, or a set of common European languages.
Step 3: find the parts that matter

OCR gives you plain text, line by line. The tool then looks through it with a few rules that match how receipts are printed: Total: the last line that says total, grand total, amount due or net payable and ends with a price. Tax: lines with GST, VAT, CGST, SGST, IGST or tax. Date: the first date in a common format, such as 14/10/2026 or 14 Oct 2026. Shop: the first real words near the top that are not an address line, phone number or the word receipt. Items: lines that end with a price and are not totals, tax, change or the payment method. Here is the same parser running live. The text on the left is what OCR might return. Edit it to see how a misread digit or a broken line changes the result.
Why rules and not a big AI model

A large vision language model could read a receipt in one go, but it would mean a download of several hundred megabytes and slow work on a phone without a GPU. Receipts are very regular, so OCR plus a few clear rules gets most of them right, quickly, on any device. When a field is wrong you fix it in a box, which is faster than arguing with a model.

Each receipt shows its photo next to editable fields for shop, date, tax and total. When they look right, you can download: A receipts CSV with one row per receipt, for expense reports. A line items CSV with every item, for budget tracking. JSON, if you want to feed it into your own scripts. Split the bill after a trip: scan the receipts, then put the totals into Expense Splitter. It works out who owes whom with the fewest payments.

Lay the receipt flat on a dark surface and shoot straight down. Use daylight or even room light, and avoid shadows from your phone. Scan thermal receipts soon. They fade within months, sometimes weeks in a hot wallet. If one is very long, take two photos and scan them as separate files.

Receipts can show your card's last digits, your address for deliveries, and where you were at what time. With OpenFile the photo is opened in your browser, read by the OCR model in your browser, and the result is shown in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing is saved after you close the tab. Check before you file OCR can confuse 5 and 6, or 1 and 7, on faded paper. Always glance at the total against the photo before you send an expense claim.

You finish a document, attach it, press send, and the mail app says the file is too large. It happens to me most often with scanned forms and slide decks exported from presentation apps. This post is a practical routine for getting a PDF under an email or upload limit without making it unreadable.
Know your limit, then leave headroom

The common limits are easy to remember. Gmail lets you attach up to 25 MB per message. Outlook.com allows 20 MB. Many company mail servers are set lower, often 10 MB, and job portals and government forms frequently cap uploads at 2 or 5 MB. There is a catch. Email is a text system, so attachments are encoded as text on the way out, which makes them roughly a third bigger in transit. Some servers count the encoded size. That is why a 24 MB file can bounce from a server that says 25 MB. I aim for about 85 percent of the stated limit and never have the problem.
Step 1: find out what is making it big

A PDF is a container. Text, fonts and vector drawings are tiny. Images are almost always the heavy part. A 40 page report of plain text might be 300 KB. The same report with a full-page photo on every page can be 60 MB. Two quick ways to check: Try selecting text in the PDF. If you cannot, each page is a picture, which means it is a scan, and scans compress very well. Open Extract PDF Images. If it finds a handful of huge images, those are your target.
Step 2: compress with the right preset

Compress PDF has four presets. Under the hood, the smart method finds every raster image in the file, downsamples it to a target resolution and recompresses it as JPEG, while leaving text and vector graphics exactly as they were. Low, about 150 DPI and quality 82: best quality, light savings. Good for photo books and anything that may be printed. Medium, about 120 DPI and quality 70: the recommended balance. Text in scans stays crisp on screen. High, about 96 DPI and quality 56: smaller, softer images. Fine for reading on a laptop. Extreme, about 72 DPI and quality 42: smallest, with visible loss. Use it when a form insists on 1 or 2 MB. If none of the presets are quite right, open Fine-tune DPI and quality and set them yourself. The tool also keeps the original whenever recompressing would make an image bigger, so it never makes things worse.
When smart compression is not enough

Some PDFs are big for reasons other than images: embedded fonts, thousands of tiny vector shapes from a CAD export, or layers of annotations. For those, switch the method to Rasterize. Every page is rendered to an image at the DPI you choose and the PDF is rebuilt from those images. The file becomes predictable in size, but the text is no longer selectable, so run OCR PDF afterwards if you need search. Rasterizing removes form fields, links and selectable text. Keep the original, and only send the rasterized copy when size matters more than those features.

Go grayscale. A scanned black and white letter saved in color wastes space. PDF to Grayscale often cuts a scan by a third before you even compress. Remove pages nobody needs. Blank pages, duplicate cover sheets and appendices add up. Remove Blank Pages finds the empty ones for you. Fix it at the source. If you are building the PDF from phone photos, shrink the photos first with Compress Image to Size, then combine them with Image to PDF. That gives you far more control than compressing afterwards.

Sometimes a document is just big. A 300 page manual with diagrams will not become 10 MB without becoming useless. In that case, split it. Split PDF has a By size mode: you enter the maximum size per file and it works out where to cut, so each part fits. Then send them as Part 1 of 3, Part 2 of 3 and so on. If you have many parts, put them in one ZIP only when the recipient asked for it. Many mail filters treat ZIP attachments with suspicion, and a ZIP of PDFs is barely smaller than the PDFs themselves because they are already compressed.

Delete pages I do not need. Grayscale, if the document has no meaningful color. Compress on Medium. Check the result. If still too big, High, then Extreme. If still too big, split by size. Each step is a separate tool, so I check the output after each one. The page thumbnails and the before and after sizes make that quick. Privacy Most online PDF compressors upload your file to a server. Contracts, payslips and medical letters are exactly the documents that end up being too big for email, so I built these tools to do all of the above inside your browser. The file never leaves your device, and you can confirm it by turning off Wi-Fi after the page loads.

For really large files, the honest answer is often a link instead of an attachment. Gmail does this automatically with Drive for big files.
