A rental agreement, a school consent form, an offer letter. Sooner or later someone sends you a PDF and says please fill this in, sign and send it back. The usual options are printing and scanning, or uploading the document to an e-signature website. This post shows the third option: doing all of it in your browser, with the file never leaving your device.
Two very different things called signing

Before the how, one distinction that confuses a lot of people. Signature image Digital signature (certificate) What it is a picture of your handwriting placed on the page cryptographic proof attached to the file What it proves that you meant to sign, like ink on paper who signed, and that nothing changed afterwards What you need a mouse, finger or pen a certificate file (.p12 or.pfx) from an issuer Typical use everyday forms, letters, rental papers contracts and official filings that require it OpenFile tool Sign PDF Digital Signature (Certificate) Most of the time people mean the first kind, and in many countries a simple electronic signature like that is accepted for everyday documents. When a document says it needs a qualified or certificate based signature, that is the second kind. If in doubt, ask whoever sent the form what they accept.
Here is a small version of the signature pad. Draw with a mouse, a finger or a stylus, then make a transparent PNG. It is drawn by your browser's canvas and stays in this tab.

Many PDFs from banks, schools and government offices have real form fields: text boxes, checkboxes, dropdowns and radio buttons. Fill PDF Form detects them, lists them in a panel next to the page, and lets you type into each one. Dropdowns show their options, checkboxes toggle, and you can see the result on the rendered page as you go. When you save, you choose between two outcomes: Keep fields editable. The values are written into the form, and anyone can still change them in a PDF reader. Good when someone else fills in the rest. Flatten. The values are merged into the page and can no longer be edited. Good for the final copy you send back.
What if the PDF has no fields

Plenty of forms are just a scanned page with lines on it. You have two options. For a one-off, open Edit PDF and add text boxes where you need them. If you send the same form to many people, make it fillable once with Create Fillable PDF Form: draw text fields, checkboxes, dropdowns and signature fields on the page, and it writes standard AcroForm fields that work in Acrobat, browsers and phone apps. Fill PDF Form can also load values from a JSON file. If you fill the same form every month with mostly the same details, save your answers once and load them next time.

Sign PDF gives you three ways to make a signature: draw it, type your name in a handwriting style font, or upload a photo of your signature on white paper. Then you click on the page to place it, drag to move it and resize it with the handles. The same tool adds the date, in the format you pick, and your initials, which many contracts want on every page. You can save a signature on this device so you do not draw it again next time. It is kept in your browser's local storage, not on a server, and you can delete it from the saved list whenever you like.

Fill the fields and keep them editable. Read the whole thing once on the page preview. Sign, add the date and initials. Flatten, so fields and annotations cannot be changed by accident. Flatten PDF does this as its own step if you need it. If the file is large, compress it last. Signing a certificate signed file If a PDF already carries a digital signature, any later change, including adding your signature image, can show up as a modification in the signer's software. When you receive a document that is already certificate signed, sign it with a certificate too, so the earlier signature stays valid as an incremental update.
Certificate signatures without uploading your key

If you have a personal or company certificate, Digital Signature (Certificate) opens your.p12 or.pfx file locally, asks for its password, and builds a SHA-256 signature over the exact bytes of the PDF. The signature can be visible, with your name and the date in a box, or invisible. It is added as an incremental update, so any signatures already in the file keep working. This is the part where privacy matters most. Your certificate file and its password are, in effect, your identity. Uploading them to a website so it can sign on your behalf is a big ask. Here they are read into memory in this tab, used once, and gone when you close it. On the receiving end, Verify PDF Signatures checks each signature in a document: whether the signed bytes still match, who signed it, the certificate chain and any timestamp. What OpenFile does not do It does not send documents to other people for signature or track who has signed. Those workflows need a server that holds the document, which is exactly what OpenFile avoids. For a single signer, which is most cases, you do not need any of that.

The Sketch board is the tool I open most when I am thinking. It is an infinite canvas for boxes, arrows, sticky notes and quick drawings, and it autosaves in your browser. These tips help you draw diagrams much faster.

Every drawing tool has a key. 1 is select, 2 is rectangle, 3 is diamond, 4 is ellipse, 5 is arrow, 6 is line, 7 is pencil, 8 is text. Once you stop reaching for the toolbar, diagrams come together quickly.
Normally a tool switches back to select after you draw one shape. Press Q to keep it active, so you can draw ten boxes in a row. Press Q again to turn it off.
Start an arrow on one shape and end it on another. The arrow binds to both, so when you move a box the arrow follows. This keeps diagrams tidy while you rearrange them.
Alt S turns snapping on. Shapes line up neatly and arrow keys move them by one grid step when you hold Shift.
Draw a frame around a part of the board and it becomes a slide. Alt P starts presenting, and arrow keys move between frames. It is a quick way to walk someone through an idea.
Export the whole board or only the selection as PNG or SVG. SVG stays sharp at any size, which is great for docs and READMEs. Press? on the board to see every shortcut at once.

Subtitles look simple: some text that shows up at the right time. Then you try to use a subtitle file from one place in another, and the player ignores it, the letters turn into question marks, or every line arrives two seconds late. This guide covers the three formats you will meet most (SRT, VTT and ASS), the problems that come up again and again, and how to fix each one in a browser tab.

SubRip is the most common subtitle format there is. Each cue is a number, a time range, one or more lines of text and a blank line. Times use a comma before the milliseconds, like 00:01:02,500. It supports basic italic and bold tags and not much else. Almost every video player and editing app reads it.

WebVTT is the web's format, and it is what the HTML video element needs. It looks almost like SRT, with three differences that matter: the file starts with the line WEBVTT, times use a dot instead of a comma, and cue numbers are optional. It adds cue settings for position and alignment, and can be styled with CSS.

Advanced SubStation Alpha is the format for subtitles that need to look a certain way: fonts, colours, outlines, positions, karaoke timing, even moving text. Anime fansubs made it famous. The file has sections for script info, named styles and events, and each dialogue line references a style. Times are in hundredths of a second. SRT VTT ASS Time format 00:00:01,000 00:00:01.000 0:00:01.00 Styling italic and bold positions, CSS classes full fonts, colours, positions, effects Works in web video no, convert to VTT yes no, convert or burn in Best for sharing, editing apps websites and web players styled or typeset subtitles
The demo turns SRT into VTT as you type, and can shift every line earlier or later. Paste a few lines from one of your own files to see it work.
Problem 1: the player will not load the file

Usually a format mismatch. A website needs VTT, a TV may only accept SRT, and a video editor might want either. Subtitle Converter converts between SRT, VTT, ASS, SSA, SBV, SUB, LRC, SAMI, TTML, JSON and CSV, in bulk, keeping timing to the millisecond. Converting from ASS to SRT or VTT drops the styling, since those formats cannot express it. The text and timing survive. Converting SRT to ASS gives every line a default style you can then change.

Older subtitle files, especially for languages with accented or non-Latin letters, were often saved in a regional encoding instead of UTF-8. Open one in a modern player and you get symbols instead of letters. The converter detects the encoding automatically and offers a picker for stubborn files. Save the result as UTF-8 and the problem is gone for good.

There are two kinds of sync problems, and they need different fixes. Subtitle Shift and Sync handles both. A constant offset. Every line is early or late by the same amount, often because the video has a different intro. A fixed shift fixes it. Drift. The first lines are right but the error grows through the film. This is almost always a frame rate mismatch, such as subtitles made for a 23.976 fps release used on a 25 fps one. Scaling by the ratio of the frame rates fixes it. If you do not know the rates, the two point method works: give the correct time for one line near the start and one near the end, and every line in between is adjusted along a straight line. To find the offset, play the video, note the exact time someone starts speaking, and compare it with the time in the subtitle file. That difference is your shift.

If the subtitles are inside the video file, as they often are in MKV files, Extract Subtitles pulls the text tracks out as SRT, VTT, ASS and more. Picture-based tracks such as PGS from Blu-ray discs are listed but are images, not text, so they need OCR. If there are no subtitles anywhere, make them. Audio Transcriber runs the Whisper speech model on your device and exports SRT directly, with optional word-level timing for short, punchy captions. Then polish the result in Subtitle Editor, which plays the video with the current line on top, lets you set times from the player, and split long lines.

The last choice is how the subtitles travel with the video. Soft subtitles are a separate track the viewer can switch on or off, either a separate file next to the video or a track inside an MP4 or MKV. They stay editable and searchable, and you can include several languages. Burned-in subtitles are drawn into the picture itself. They show up everywhere, including social apps that ignore subtitle tracks, but nobody can turn them off or fix a typo later. Add Subtitles to Video does both. It burns subtitles in with libass, the same renderer many desktop players use, so ASS styling comes through, or it adds them as a switchable track in MP4 or MKV without re-encoding the video, which is nearly instant. Translation To reach more viewers, Subtitle Translator translates SRT, VTT or ASS files into more than 50 languages on your device with the NLLB-200 model, one line at a time, so the timing never changes. The model is a large one-time download, so do it on Wi-Fi.
My usual flow for a talk recording

Transcribe with Whisper base, export SRT. Fix names and technical terms in the Subtitle Editor. Convert to VTT for the website player. Burn a copy in for the social media clip. All four steps run in the browser, so an unreleased recording stays on my laptop the whole time.

Editing video in a browser tab used to sound like a joke. Today it works well for most everyday jobs: trimming a clip, shrinking a file for chat, making a GIF. Here is how it works in OpenFile and how to get the best speed out of it.

ffmpeg is the open-source tool behind a huge share of the world's video software. It is written in C. With a compiler called Emscripten, that C code becomes WebAssembly, a compact binary format that browsers run at close to native speed. So when you trim a video in OpenFile, real ffmpeg is running inside your tab. Your file is placed in a small in-memory file system, ffmpeg reads it, writes the result, and the page hands it back to you.
Why the first run is slower
The ffmpeg engine is about 30 MB. The first time you open a video tool, your browser downloads it once. After that it is cached, and the service worker keeps it available offline.
Speed depends on a few browser features. The demo below checks them on your device.

Trim first. Every second you cut is a second ffmpeg does not have to encode. Copy streams when you can. If you only cut a clip and keep the format, the trimmer can copy the streams without re-encoding. That is nearly instant. Lower the resolution. 720p encodes roughly twice as fast as 1080p. Keep the tab visible. Browsers slow down background tabs to save power. Plug in your laptop. Power saving modes reduce CPU speed a lot.

Very long 4K videos are still better handled by a desktop app. A tab has less memory to work with, and WebAssembly cannot yet use every hardware trick a native app can. For clips up to a few minutes, the browser is more than enough.

After a CT or MRI scan, many hospitals hand you a CD or a download link full of files with names like IM000123 and no extension. Double-click one and nothing happens. Those are DICOM files, and they are perfectly viewable if you know what they are. This post explains the format, the one control that matters most, and how to look at your own scans without uploading them to a stranger's website. Not for diagnosis OpenFile's DICOM Viewer is for education and convenience, so you can see your own images or share a picture with family. It is not a certified medical device. Your radiologist's report is what counts.

DICOM stands for Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine. It is both a file format and a network protocol, and nearly every scanner, hospital archive and medical viewer speaks it. A DICOM file holds two things: Tags: hundreds of labelled fields, each with a numeric id. Patient name, birth date, the hospital, the scanner model, slice thickness, the position of the slice in the body, and much more. Pixel data: the image itself, often 12 or 16 bits per pixel instead of the 8 bits of a normal photo. A single CT scan is not one file. It is a series: usually one file per slice, sometimes hundreds of them, which together make up a 3D volume. That is why opening one file in isolation feels like looking at a single page torn from a book.

Here is the part that surprised me most. In a CT image, a pixel does not store a brightness. It stores a measurement: how strongly that bit of tissue absorbed X-rays, on the Hounsfield scale. Water is 0, air is about minus 1000, fat is around minus 100, soft tissue sits roughly between 20 and 80, and dense bone goes up to well over a thousand. That range is far wider than a screen can show in 256 shades of grey. So viewers use a window: you pick a centre value (the level) and a width, and only values inside that range are spread from black to white. Everything below is black, everything above is white. Try it on the made-up slice below. The presets are the same ones the viewer offers. Notice how the Lung preset shows the inside of the lungs but turns everything else into a white blob, while Soft tissue does the opposite. Same pixels, different window. Radiologists switch windows constantly for exactly this reason.

DICOM Viewer reads DICOM with dicom-parser, and also opens NIfTI and NRRD volumes, which are common in research and teaching. Find the folder with the image files. On a hospital CD there is often a DICOM folder with many subfolders. Each subfolder is usually one series. Select all the files of a series and drop them in together. The viewer sorts slices by their instance number and stacks them. Drag on the image to change window and level. Scroll, or use the arrow keys, to move through the slices. Use the CT presets (Soft tissue, Lung, Bone and Brain) as a starting point, and Invert if you prefer bones dark. Save the current slice, or all slices, as PNG.

Scanners often store raw numbers and two tags that convert them into real units. The viewer applies this rescale automatically, so the values under your cursor are true Hounsfield units for CT. You do not need to do anything, but it explains why another tool might show different numbers for the same pixel.

Because DICOM files carry names, dates of birth and hospital details inside them, I treat them like any other medical record. A few habits: The viewer shows the key tags in a details panel, and you can hide them with Hide patient data before you take a screenshot. Exported PNGs contain only pixels. No patient tags are written into them, which makes PNG the right format for sending a picture to a relative. Never send the original DICOM files to someone who does not need them. They carry far more than the picture. If a screenshot shows burned-in text on the image itself, some scanners print the name in a corner, cover it with Blur and Redact Image before sharing. Want a single document for a second opinion appointment? Export the few slices that matter as PNG, then combine them with Image to PDF. It prints well and opens on any device.

Search for an online DICOM viewer and many of the results upload your files to a server to process them. For a scan of your head or chest, that is a lot of personal health information to hand over to a site you found a minute ago. With OpenFile the files are parsed in your browser tab, the pixels are drawn on a canvas, and nothing is sent anywhere. You can load the page, turn off Wi-Fi, and keep working. Limits Compressed DICOM transfer syntaxes vary a lot between scanners. Most common CT, MRI and X-ray files open fine. If a series does not, the hospital's own viewer on the CD is the safest fallback, and the radiology department can usually export a standard copy on request.

If you run, ride or swim with a watch or a bike computer, every workout ends up as a small file with a.fit extension. Most people never see it, because the watch app syncs it away. But that file is yours, and it holds far more than the summary screen shows. I wrote a FIT reader for OpenFile this week, so here is what is inside one, how to turn it into a spreadsheet or GPX, and how to read heart rate zones from it without signing up for anything.

FIT means Flexible and Interoperable Data Transfer. Garmin created it, and today Wahoo, Coros, Suunto, Hammerhead, Zwift and many others use it too. It is a binary format, so you cannot open it in a text editor, and it is built to be small: an hour of riding with GPS, heart rate, cadence and power is often only a few hundred kilobytes. The file starts with a 12 or 14 byte header and the letters.FIT. After that come messages. There are two kinds. A definition message says "messages of local type 1 will have these fields, in this order, with these sizes". Data messages then carry only the values, with no names, which is why the format is so compact.

Message What it holds file_id Who made the file: maker, product, when it was created record One sample, usually every second: time, position, altitude, heart rate, cadence, speed, power, temperature lap Each lap or auto lap: start, time, distance, average and max heart rate session The whole activity: sport, total time, distance, calories, climb event, device_info, hrv Start and stop, sensor details, beat to beat intervals

Some values are stored in unusual ways to save space. Positions are in semicircles: a 32 bit number where 2 to the power of 31 means 180 degrees. Altitude is stored times 5 plus 500, so it never goes negative. Speed is millimetres per second. Time counts seconds since the last day of 1989, not since 1970 like most computers. Some devices also use a compressed timestamp that keeps only the last 5 bits of the time in the record header. A reader has to handle all of this, or your run ends up in the ocean in the year 2009.

FIT File Converter and Viewer reads the file in your browser and shows the sport, distance, time, pace, heart rate, climb and power, the shape of the route, and charts for heart rate, elevation, speed and power. Then you can download: CSV: one row per sample with clear column names, ready for a spreadsheet or a notebook. GPX: the route with heart rate and cadence, for mapping apps and sites that do not take FIT. Excel: samples on one sheet and laps on another. JSON: everything, for your own scripts. It also opens TCX and GPX files, so you can use the same viewer for exports from other apps. Where to find the files: on Garmin devices, plug in by USB and look in the Garmin/Activity folder. In most watch apps and web dashboards, the activity menu has Export Original or Export FIT.
Heart rate zones in plain words

Zones are bands of heart rate that match different kinds of effort. The common five zone model is based on your maximum heart rate: Zone 1, easy: 50 to 60 percent of max. Warm up and recovery. Zone 2, endurance: 60 to 70 percent. Long easy runs and rides. You can talk. Zone 3, tempo: 70 to 80 percent. Steady and a bit uncomfortable. Zone 4, threshold: 80 to 90 percent. Hard intervals. Zone 5, max: above 90 percent. Short, all out efforts. Another way, called heart rate reserve or the Karvonen method, uses the gap between your resting and max heart rate. It moves the zones up a little for people with a low resting rate. Play with the sliders below to see both. The age formula is only a starting point. Real max heart rates vary a lot between people of the same age. If you have seen a higher number on a hard climb or a race finish, use that instead.
Time in zone and training load

Heart Rate Zones takes a workout file and adds up the seconds you spent in each zone. Pauses longer than 30 seconds count as 30, so a coffee stop does not fill your zone 1. It also works out a training load score called TRIMP, from Eric Banister. Each minute is weighted by how close you were to your max, with a curve that grows quickly at high effort. So 30 minutes of hard intervals can score more than an hour of easy jogging, which matches how tired you feel the next day. Not medical advice These numbers are for training. If something feels wrong with your heart, see a doctor, not a chart.

If your data lives in the Apple Health app instead, Apple Health Export to CSV opens the export.zip from the Health app. That file can be several gigabytes, so the tool reads it in 4 MB pieces and never loads it all at once. You get one CSV per type, for example steps, heart rate, weight and workouts, plus a daily total or average for each.

Workout files show where you live, the routes you take, and when you leave home. Uploading them to a random converter is a real privacy risk. OpenFile reads them inside your browser. Nothing is uploaded, and there is no account to make.
